title: MoD Documents: UK Police Erred in Ceding Airbase Assault Case to US Military
description: Internal ministry documents say Cambridgeshire police should not have handed the investigation of a US fighter pilot to American military authorities, as a cross-government inquiry examines how serious crimes involving US personnel end up outside British courts.
body: Ministry of Defence officials have privately concluded that Cambridgeshire police should not have allowed the US military to take control of the investigation into an American fighter pilot accused of assaulting a British woman, according to documents obtained by the Guardian and published on 31 October. The officials said the force should “absolutely” not have surrendered the case, describing the handover as a clear breach of a long-established agreement governing how the two countries handle alleged crimes by US personnel stationed in Britain. The case centres on Capt Jacob Wulfson, who was accused of sexually assaulting Sarah Steele in his Cambridge flat in December 2023 after the pair met on the Tinder dating app. Rather than face an English criminal court, Wulfson was prosecuted in a military tribunal on a US airbase in neighbouring Suffolk. The Guardian reports that all the lawyers involved in that proceeding were American. The documents add a formal, internal dimension to a dispute that became public in June, when the Guardian first disclosed the case. Downing Street responded at the time by calling it “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that UK authorities had not been involved in prosecuting Wulfson, and the government announced a high-level inquiry into how and why police forces have been transferring investigations into serious crimes to US military police. The Ministry of Defence, which manages the military relationship with Washington, is one of the key departments taking part, alongside the Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office. The jurisdictional question at the heart of the case is not ambiguous on paper. Under the terms of the UK-US agreement, police in Britain have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes by Americans stationed in the country. The MoD officials' assessment, as reported, is that Cambridgeshire police gave up that right when they let US military police quickly assume control of the Wulfson investigation. The practical effect was that a British complainant's allegation was adjudicated inside a US military system, on a US airbase, rather than through the Crown Prosecution Service and the English courts. Cambridgeshire police have not accepted the characterisation directly. The force said it is conducting a review of the case with what it called “the assistance of material provided” by US Air Force lawyers, and that it “remained engaged with the victim.” It added that it is “working with government, wider policing and criminal justice partners to ensure greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making.” That language points to a process problem — unclear decision-making at the point where a local force decides whether to assert or waive its primacy — rather than to a single disputed judgement. The Wulfson case is not the only one feeding the inquiry. The Guardian's reporting references Tyrion Davis, who allegedly raped two women in Suffolk. He was convicted of one charge of sexual assault but cleared of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact. The details of how that case was handled, and by whom, are not fully set out in the available material, but its inclusion signals that the inquiry is looking at a pattern rather than an isolated incident. The scale of the underlying relationship helps explain why the issue has become politically sensitive. The US has more than 12,000 military personnel in the UK, stationed at at least 15 bases and facilities. Those personnel live and work in British communities, and allegations involving them can arise in ordinary civilian settings — a flat in Cambridge, a town in Suffolk — where local police are the first responders. The agreement that governs those encounters is meant to balance two interests: the US military's desire to maintain discipline and prosecute its own people, and the UK's interest in ensuring that crimes committed on British soil are investigated and tried under British law. The US military, according to the reporting, aims to prosecute as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK. That is an institutional incentive, not necessarily a legal entitlement, and the boundary is precisely what is in dispute. Where US authorities assert jurisdiction and UK police acquiesce, the agreement's primacy provision becomes effectively unenforced. The MoD documents suggest that at least some officials inside the department responsible for the relationship believe that is what happened in the Wulfson case. The political timeline matters. The case became public in June, prompting criticism from Downing Street and the establishment of the cross-government inquiry. The inquiry's remit is broad: it is examining how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts. That framing implies the government accepts there is a systemic issue, even as individual forces and the MoD may disagree about where responsibility lies in any given case. The MoD documents reported on 31 October sharpen that question by putting a departmental judgement on record: the force, in the officials' view, got it wrong. For Sarah Steele, the practical consequences are already settled in one sense — the prosecution happened in a US tribunal, not an English court, and no British prosecution now looms. What the inquiry can change is the handling of future cases. The variables it can influence are procedural: whether police forces receive clearer guidance on when they must assert primacy; whether the MoD, Home Office and Crown Prosecution Service establish a notification or review mechanism before a case is handed to US military police; and whether victims are told, in plain terms, which legal system will handle their allegation and what rights they have in it. There are limits to what the public record currently establishes. The documents obtained by the Guardian are described in the reporting, but their full text, the identity of the officials quoted, and the precise legal reasoning behind the “clear breach” assessment are not set out in the available material. It is also not established whether the MoD's view has been formally conveyed to Cambridgeshire police, whether the force disputes it, or whether the inquiry has reached interim conclusions. The US Air Force's position on the handover is not detailed beyond the general statement that the US military seeks to prosecute its personnel within the agreement's boundaries. The case also sits inside a wider question about accountability that predates it. Status-of-forces arrangements are common among allied militaries, and they routinely allocate investigative and prosecutorial responsibility. Disputes tend to arise not over the text but over early-stage practice — who arrives first, who controls evidence, who interviews the complainant, and who decides that a case is “theirs.” Those decisions are often made by officers on the ground under time pressure, which is why the inquiry's focus on “jurisdictional decision making” is likely to produce recommendations about training and escalation rather than about the treaty itself. For the government, the political risk is twofold. If the inquiry concludes that police forces routinely ceded cases they should have kept, ministers will face questions about why guidance was not clearer and why oversight was absent. If it concludes that the Wulfson handover was an isolated error, the broader criticism — that British victims of US personnel can end up outside British courts — will not be fully answered. The MoD documents push the evidence toward the first conclusion, at least for this case. What is not in doubt is the sequence. A woman reported an assault in Cambridge in December 2023. US military police took control of the investigation. A US military tribunal on a Suffolk airbase tried the case. British police did not prosecute. In October, MoD officials said, according to the documents, that they should not have let that happen. The inquiry now has to decide what changes. The case tests whether the UK's primacy right under its status-of-forces agreement with the US is real in practice. If local police can hand serious cases to US military police without challenge, British victims' access to English courts depends on decisions made by officers under time pressure, with little visible oversight. The MoD's internal judgement shifts the question from a single disputed case to whether guidance, notification and review mechanisms are adequate across all forces hosting US personnel. The cross-government inquiry, involving the MoD, Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office, is expected to examine how cases are transferred and may recommend clearer rules on asserting primacy. Cambridgeshire police's review, conducted with material from US Air Force lawyers, could produce its own findings. The political pressure point is whether ministers publish inquiry conclusions and whether guidance to forces changes before the next high-profile case arises. The MoD documents and police language about 'greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making' both point to a procedural fix rather than a treaty renegotiation. By mid-2027 The inquiry reports without publishing case-level findings, and the Wulfson matter is treated as an isolated error rather than evidence of a systemic pattern. Governments often limit disclosure in cases touching allied military arrangements; the inquiry's remit is broad but its output may be narrow. By end-2027 A further case involving US personnel and a British complainant becomes public, renewing pressure and prompting faster ministerial action. With more than 12,000 US personnel at 15-plus sites, the underlying conditions for such cases persist regardless of the inquiry. Next 12 months

title: Molly, a Signal fork, has gone three months without an update, leaving known fixes unpatched
description: A community post says the fork's last release was v8.19.2-4 on 31 July and recommends switching to mainline Signal until Molly resumes regular updates.
body: Molly, a hardened fork of the Signal messaging app, has not shipped a release since 31 July, when version v8.19.2-4 was published, according to a community post on piefed.world dated 31 October. The post says the fork therefore lacks fixes that have already landed in mainline Signal, and it recommends that users switch to the official Signal client and delete Molly until the project resumes updating the app adequately, "if they ever will." The claim rests on a single community write-up rather than a published security advisory, a coordinated disclosure or a statement from the Molly maintainers. The post does not name the specific vulnerabilities, cite CVE identifiers, describe the attack conditions under which they could be exploited, or say which mainline Signal versions contain the corresponding fixes. It also does not say whether Molly's maintainers have announced a pause, a handover or an end to the project. Those gaps matter for anyone deciding whether to keep using the fork. The underlying concern is structural rather than exotic. A fork copies a codebase and then diverges from it. When the upstream project patches a flaw, the fork only benefits if its maintainers pull in the change, rebuild and publish. A three-month gap between Molly's last release and the current date means any security fixes merged into Signal during that window are, by the post's account, absent from the fork. The post frames the situation as one where fixes were "simply fixed" upstream while Molly "remains vulnerable." Molly has been positioned as a privacy-focused alternative to Signal, and forks of messaging apps tend to attract users who want hardening or features the mainline client does not offer. That same audience is exposed when the fork's release cadence slips, because the security properties of a messaging client depend on staying current with upstream patches. The post's recommendation is blunt: use mainline Signal and remove Molly in the interim. What the available material does not establish is the practical severity. Without named vulnerabilities, it is not possible to say from this source alone whether the unpatched issues require a remote attacker, local access, a malicious contact or some other precondition, or whether they affect the encryption protocol itself versus the app's surrounding code. The post asserts vulnerability but supplies no technical detail, and no second source in this evidence set corroborates the release date or the security assessment. For users, the decision hinges on facts the post leaves open: whether Molly's maintainers have published a roadmap, whether a release is imminent, and whether the fork's build process tracks upstream closely enough that a delayed release still contains recent fixes. None of that is answered here. The post's own hedge, "if they ever will," signals that even its author is uncertain about the project's future. The safer reading of the evidence is narrow. A community post says Molly's last release was 31 July and that the fork is missing fixes present in mainline Signal. That claim is unverified by a second source and undetailed as to the vulnerabilities themselves. title: AI writing detectors flagged a 20-year professional. She lost the book proposal.
description: NPR reports that detection tools can disagree sharply on the same text, and that writers are now changing how they write to avoid being accused.
body: A nonfiction writer with more than 20 years of professional experience submitted writing samples for a book proposal and got back an email saying several artificial intelligence detection tools had flagged her work as machine-generated. She had not used AI to produce the text, she told NPR, and she believes the detector results cost her the chance to write the full proposal. NPR identifies the writer as McGraw. She was paid for the samples, she said, but was angry that her work had been dismissed as machine output. The client confirmed to NPR that she had screened McGraw's writing for AI. McGraw described her reaction as a physical one, saying her ears burned with anger. The case sits inside a broader problem in publishing and education, where software is increasingly used to judge whether text came from a person or a machine. NPR reports that researchers have found different AI detection tools can reach dramatically different conclusions about the same piece of writing. That variance matters because the tools are being used as gatekeepers, not merely as advisory checks. One measure of the pressure comes from a science fiction magazine. Clarke, its publisher, told NPR that submissions doubled by February 2023, after AI agents such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini became widely available, forcing the magazine to temporarily close its submission portal. He estimates his own workload has risen by about 30%, and he said the flood of AI-assisted submissions has introduced mistrust into the process. Clarke said he does not personally use AI detectors to screen incoming manuscripts, but he thinks certain detection tools could help overwhelmed editors manage volume, provided they check the detector's findings. He cautioned against turning suspicion into accusation, arguing that a submission should end in a rejection rather than a charge against the writer. NPR's reporting includes a test of four detectors on 40 papers. Pangram was the most consistently accurate among the four, correctly identifying AI use in 37 of the 40 papers with combined text and in 37 of the 40 where a human rewrote AI-generated text. Pangram CEO Max Spero said in an emailed statement that his company's detector can make mistakes, particularly when there is not much writing to evaluate. The mechanics of detection help explain the errors. Chris Callison-Burch, a professor of computer and information science at the University of Pennsylvania, told NPR that many AI detectors work by asking a large language model how predictable a passage is. Previously published writing can pose an additional problem, he said. An unpublished draft like McGraw's sample would not face that particular issue, but could still be falsely flagged based on patterns in the writer's style. NPR reported one detector's output as a 98.7% confidence that a passage was machine-generated, a figure that shows how precise the tools can sound even when their judgments are contested. The Authors Guild, which advocates for writers' rights, said in May that the use of AI detectors has created an atmosphere of suspicion, with writers worried about false accusations and about how to defend themselves. McGraw said the fear of another accusation has changed how she writes. She now avoids certain words and sentence constructions and occasionally leaves out commas she used to include, hoping the inconsistency will help show that a human wrote the text. She also said it is widely understood that these screeners are not fully accurate. Teachers are using software to check whether students used AI, NPR notes, extending the same accuracy questions into classrooms where a false positive can carry academic consequences. The practical difficulty for anyone accused is that detection output rarely arrives with an explanation a writer can rebut. A confidence score is not evidence of authorship, and the tools' disagreement with one another gives accused writers little clear ground to stand on. Publishers and editors facing rising submission volumes have reason to want filters, but the NPR reporting shows the filters can misread experienced human prose and that at least one detector's own chief executive acknowledges limits on short samples. For now, the burden is falling on writers to prove a negative, and some are pre-emptively altering their style to look less machine-like. Detection tools are being used as gatekeepers in publishing and education, so their error rate is not abstract. A false positive can cost a writer paid work or a student an academic record, and the accused often have no way to audit the score. The NPR reporting shows the tools disagree with each other and that at least one vendor acknowledges mistakes on short samples, which shifts risk onto people who did nothing wrong. Writers are already changing word choice and punctuation to avoid suspicion, a behavioral cost that does not show up in accuracy statistics. Expect more institutions to adopt detectors as submission volumes rise, and expect pushback from writers' groups and possibly from institutions facing appeals. Vendors may respond with documentation features or human-review guidance, though nothing in the reporting confirms such plans. The near-term pattern is likely to be uneven: some editors use detectors as a first filter with manual checks, while others avoid them. Legal or contractual challenges are possible but not established. title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
description: Ars Technica reports that long-distance seabird flights home may disrupt the birds' internal clocks, a finding with implications for how researchers interpret migration timing.
body: Ars Technica reports that seabirds racing home across the ocean can experience something akin to jet lag, according to a report published on October 31, 2026. The finding concerns the mismatch between a bird's internal body clock and the light cues it encounters as it travels long distances across time zones or shifting day lengths. The available source material is limited to the headline and a small set of extracted facts, which do not include the underlying study, the species involved, the number of birds tracked, the measurement methods or the specific physiological results. What can be reported is the central claim: seabirds making rapid return journeys over the ocean may face a disruption to their circadian timing comparable to the disorientation travelers experience after crossing time zones. Jet lag in humans arises when the body's internal clock, which regulates sleep, alertness and metabolism, falls out of step with local daylight. Recovery typically requires gradual adjustment to the new light-dark cycle. The Ars Technica report suggests a similar mechanism may apply to seabirds whose fast homeward flights carry them across changing light conditions faster than their internal clocks can reset. Why this would matter for seabirds is not spelled out in the supplied material. Plausible consequences, which the source does not confirm, include effects on foraging, navigation, predator avoidance or the timing of arrival at breeding colonies. The report does not provide figures on how long any disruption lasts or whether it affects survival or reproduction. The source also does not identify the researchers, institution or journal behind the work, nor the dates or locations of the tracking. Those details would be needed to assess the strength of the claim and how broadly it applies across seabird species. Until fuller reporting is available, the report should be read as a description of a proposed phenomenon rather than a quantified result. The core assertion is that rapid homeward ocean crossings can desynchronize seabirds' internal clocks, and that this deserves attention in studies of migration and at-sea behavior. If rapid homeward flights genuinely disrupt seabird circadian timing, the effect would matter most for birds arriving at breeding colonies, where timing affects mate competition, nest initiation and chick-rearing schedules. It would also matter for researchers who use arrival dates and at-sea behavior as indicators of environmental change, because clock disruption could confound those signals. The claim remains unquantified in the supplied material, so its practical weight is uncertain. Expect the underlying study to circulate among ornithologists and migration ecologists, with scrutiny focused on sample size, species coverage and whether physiological markers of clock disruption were measured directly or inferred from behavior. Follow-up work would likely test whether recovery time varies with flight speed, distance and light conditions, and whether arrival timing or breeding success is measurably affected. title: Healey threatens veto on offshore wind projects that do not cut bills
description: The chancellor says ministers will only sign off new subsidy contracts if the grid can absorb the power without raising consumer costs, as a £3bn energy budget cut sharpens questions about Labour's clean power target.
body: John Healey has said he will veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills, a position that adds to concerns the government is stepping back from its pro-renewables agenda. Under the approach he described, new offshore wind projects bidding for subsidy contracts would only be signed off by ministers if they believe all the power generated could be carried by Britain's electricity grid without pushing up costs for consumers. The condition targets a specific cost problem. The National Energy System Operator (Neso), which is funded through energy bills, must pay wind turbines to switch off when there is not enough cabling capacity to move their power to consumers. Those constraint payments show up on bills. A National Audit Office report in September warned that homes and businesses could face a potential annual bill of £7.8bn by 2030 to deal with the issue. The veto threat lands alongside budget decisions that have already unsettled parts of the government's energy programme. Healey revealed more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department's budget, much of which will pay for higher defence spending. He announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments. The Guardian reported that the combination appears to be a further shift away from Labour's target of having clean power by 2030. Allies of Ed Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government's green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed to Healey's announcement of a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and onto taxpayers, something the two energy secretaries have both championed. The government also has a target to raise a scheme's uptake to 250,000 a year by 2030 and was planning to increase its funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30. The immediate question is how the test would work in practice. Ministers would be judging whether a project's full output could be accommodated without raising consumer costs, a standard that depends on grid capacity that is not yet built and on how constraint costs are forecast. The government has not set out, in the reporting available, the threshold it would apply or which projects might fail it. The veto threat shifts risk onto offshore wind developers and their supply chains. A project that wins a subsidy contract but cannot show its output will be absorbed without raising bills now faces ministerial rejection, which changes how developers size and site schemes and how they model grid connection dates. For households, the policy is aimed at the constraint payments that Neso currently passes through to bills, with the NAO putting a potential £7.8bn annual cost by 2030. For the government, the £3bn energy budget cut and the bill-focused test put two priorities in tension: cutting consumer costs and keeping the pace needed for clean power by 2030. Ministers are likely to face early tests when the next round of subsidy contract decisions reaches sign-off, and developers will be watching whether the grid-capacity condition is applied strictly or used as leverage to renegotiate. The clean power 2030 target is already under pressure from the budget cuts, so the next budget and energy department spending plans will show whether the shift is rhetorical or structural. Expect more detail on how constraint costs are forecast and who bears them. title: Starmer: UK must move closer to Europe as US ties shift under Trump
description: In his first major political intervention since leaving No 10, Keir Starmer said the change in the US relationship is unlikely to reverse after Trump, and that a stronger Europe needs Britain at its heart.
body: Keir Starmer used his first significant political intervention since leaving Downing Street to argue that the UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the United States becomes a less reliable partner. Speaking at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday, the former prime minister said a stronger Europe was vital and that the UK had to be at its heart. Starmer warned European leaders about the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump's presidency was not likely to reset once Trump leaves the Oval Office. He accused European leaders of having been caught out by these new realities twice already. "Things will not go back to the way they were before," he said, according to The Guardian. The remarks mark a sharper public position than the one Starmer struck three months earlier, when, amid Trump's war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, he described Europe as a "partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together." At that time he said the ties should go beyond defence, that Brexit had done "deep damage" to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be "more ambitious," including pursuing "closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation." His successor, Andy Burnham, has also signalled a more pro-European direction. Soon after taking office, Burnham said he intended to be "bolder" about closer ties with the EU, and he has said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. The government's current posture was on display this week at a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris, where Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said they were "united and unwavering" in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility. Streeting described the UK as a leading Nato member pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine. Starmer's intervention places the argument about the US relationship and Europe's security architecture inside British domestic politics, at a moment when both the former and current prime ministers are pushing in the same general direction. The Guardian reports that Starmer framed the change in Washington's posture as structural rather than tied to one president, a claim that goes further than simply criticising Trump's conduct. The evidence available does not detail any new policy proposals from Starmer, nor does it specify what "closer" cooperation would mean in trade, defence procurement or movement of people. Burnham's call for a public debate after the next election suggests the timing of any formal shift remains open. The intervention matters most for British domestic politics and for how European capitals read London's reliability. Starmer is arguing that the US shift is structural, not a Trump-specific episode, which if accepted by the current government would raise the political cost of treating Washington as the default anchor and lower the cost of deeper EU alignment on defence and economic cooperation. Burnham's stated intent to be "bolder" and his call for a public debate after the next election give that argument an institutional path, while Streeting's Paris remarks show the government already leaning on European defence coordination for Ukraine. Expect the debate to stay rhetorical in the near term, with Starmer and Burnham testing how far pro-European language can go before concrete commitments are demanded. The next observable steps are likely to be Burnham's framing of the post-election debate, any government language on EU security or economic cooperation, and whether Streeting's Paris coordination produces joint commitments on Ukraine. title: Sherrock beats world No 1 Littler on Netflix's live darts show
description: Fallon Sherrock defeated Luke Littler on Beat Luke Littler at Manchester Central, a result the streamer had planned contingency programming for in case the world champion fell early.
body: Fallon Sherrock beat Luke Littler, the world darts No 1, on Netflix's live programme Beat Luke Littler at a packed Manchester Central arena, the Guardian reported. The show, hosted by Gary Lineker and Richard Osman, was built around the possibility that someone could take on the world champion; Sherrock did exactly that. Netflix had no guarantee when or whether Littler would be beaten, according to the Guardian, and had put contingency plans in place for a second-place competition in case he lost within the first few rounds. That planning indicates the producers treated an early exit by the headline player as a live possibility rather than a remote one. Sherrock's participation had drawn some controversy when it was revealed earlier in October. She holds an MBE for services to darts, and critics argued she was not a true amateur given her appearances at the PDC World Darts Championship and her win in the inaugural Women's World Matchplay in 2022. The Guardian reported that background without resolving the dispute. After the win in Manchester, Sherrock described the period leading up to it as difficult. "I mean, it's been tough," she said. Speaking to Lineker, she added: "I can't put into words how much this means." The Guardian reported that the result was greeted with huge cheers from the audience and a hug from her young son. The programme was a risk for the streamer, the Guardian reported, but sources said audience numbers stayed steady despite competition from The Celebrity Traitors on the BBC, and appeared to rise after the BBC show ended. Viewers could vote on the order in which players appeared. Workerbee's managing director, Michelle Chappell, told the Guardian that the idea came from CEO Rick Murray: "Wouldn't it be amazing if someone could take on Luke Littler." Chappell described the format as "a sport event but a big show at the same time" with "a sense of humour and real jeopardy." One winner was guaranteed in the scheduling battle between Beat Luke Littler and The Celebrity Traitors: Banijay, the global production company that owns the companies making both shows, according to the Guardian. The Guardian's report does not give the final score, the stage of the competition at which Sherrock beat Littler, or confirmed audience figures for the broadcast. Those details were not available in the supplied material. A live Netflix event built around one star carries concentrated risk: if Littler exits early, the format has to hold without him. The Guardian's reporting that contingency programming existed, and that audience numbers held steady against The Celebrity Traitors, suggests the producers designed for that scenario rather than assuming the champion would stay in. For Sherrock, beating the world No 1 on a mainstream streaming broadcast raises her profile beyond darts audiences, though the earlier debate over her amateur status shows that her record invites scrutiny as well as attention. For Netflix, the result is a test of whether a single-match celebrity format can absorb an upset and still draw viewers. title: TechCrunch reviewer took two iPhones on vacation; the $2K Duo won out
description: Sarah Perez carried the foldable iPhone Duo alongside her iPhone 17 Pro Max as a safety net. She used the Duo more, and came home not wanting to switch back.
body: TechCrunch's Sarah Perez spent a five-day vacation carrying two phones: the new foldable iPhone Duo and her iPhone 17 Pro Max. She had packed the Pro Max as a safety net after the Duo arrived just as she was leaving. By the end of the trip, she wrote, she was using the Duo more and did not want to go back. The Duo costs about $2,000, and Perez wrote that in the days before its ship date she had started doing the math on upgrade options that would let her afford one. She said she hesitated over both the price and the scale of the change from a high-end slab phone to what she described as a more experimental device. She framed the move as carrying a psychological switching cost beyond the sticker price. Her frustrations were concrete. Some apps were not yet optimized for the Duo, though she noted companies have been pushing out Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly and that "more than a few" apps still had not. Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet she said she had no trouble using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, and route planning. She expects the major apps to update eventually. The bigger complaint was authentication. The Duo lacks Face ID, and Perez called that its biggest drawback, ahead of the screen, the camera and the absence of an Action button for launching an AI assistant. Returning to Touch ID at payment time was cumbersome when her hands were full with shopping bags, a purse or a dog leash. She found the easiest grip was to cradle the phone and authenticate with a thumb. On cameras, she was direct about the gap. The Duo has two rear cameras to the Pro Max's three, no telephoto lens, and 10x digital zoom against the Pro's 40x. She still described foldables as whimsical in a way slab phones are not, and said Apple appears to have taken its time on the details, from a barely visible crease to a consistent aspect ratio between screens so content scales proportionally. The Duo also sits inside Apple's software ecosystem, which she said matters for people who move between Apple devices and services and pay for iOS-specific apps. Durability came up in the context of the beach. Perez wrote that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 was rated IP48 by comparison, and that she does not expect the Duo to have the same issues, though she hoped a reviewer would take it to the beach soon. She also said she had roughly half a dozen conversations with strangers on vacation, from fellow shoppers to servers to business owners, and expects that attention to diminish as the novelty wears off. She is certain at least one of those strangers had never seen a folding phone before, and argued that Apple shipping one means the concept will no longer be niche but known to the mainstream. The account is a single reviewer's experience over five days, not a lab test or a durability trial. It captures the trade-offs a buyer weighing a $2,000 foldable against a mature flagship actually faces: app readiness, biometric convenience, camera range and the social friction of a new form factor. A $2,000 foldable only sells if people who already own a top-tier iPhone decide the form factor is worth losing Face ID, a telephoto lens and full app optimization. Perez's account suggests the switching cost is real but surmountable for at least some buyers, which matters to Apple's pricing and to developers deciding how fast to ship Duo-specific updates. It also matters to rivals: if Apple normalizes folding phones, Samsung and others face a mainstream competitor in a category they spent years building alone. Watch whether the app gap Perez described closes. She expects major apps to update, and the pace of those releases will shape how quickly the Duo feels like a normal phone rather than an experiment. Durability reporting, particularly sand and water exposure at beaches, is the other open question, since she flagged the IP rating comparison with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 without testing it herself. title: FDA Moves to Withdraw Tavneos Approval Over Manipulated Trial Data
description: The agency says ChemoCentryx re-adjudicated pivotal trial results after unblinding. Amgen, which bought the company for nearly $4 billion, now argues the drug should stay on the market.
body: The US Food and Drug Administration has proposed withdrawing its approval of Tavneos, a treatment for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis, after concluding that the drug's pivotal trial data were manipulated, Ars Technica reports. The agency set out its position in an April letter to Amgen, which acquired Tavneos developer ChemoCentryx in 2022. The dispute traces back to May 2021, when the FDA released a lengthy briefing document on the experimental medication ahead of an advisory committee meeting. The agency was undecided on approval and wanted outside input, including on whether the drug was meaningfully better than existing therapies. Trial participants appeared to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year, but the FDA said the results were hard to interpret because the study design was less than optimal. One reviewer said the drug's effect was "just not well verified by this study." The advisory committee voted narrowly to recommend approval, and the FDA greenlit Tavneos on October 7, 2021. A year later, Amgen bought ChemoCentryx for nearly $4 billion. Tavneos sales reached nearly half a billion dollars in fiscal year 2025. According to the FDA, the problem lies in how ChemoCentryx handled the trial data. The company's own original analysis found that patients receiving Tavneos had not achieved better one-year remission rates than those on the usual treatment. Employees then unblinded the data, seeing which participants had received the drug and which had received a placebo, and selected a handful of patients whose remission status would be reassessed. The FDA says this re-adjudication violated the study protocol. The evidence surfaced in part through a long-running investor lawsuit, which the FDA now credits with uncovering what it considers proof of data manipulation in the pivotal trial. A court hearing was expected on October 29 to consider a proposed $69 million settlement in that case. Amgen has pushed back. In a 104-page document submitted to the FDA this summer, the company said ChemoCentryx's re-adjudication does not "align with the approach Amgen would have taken" and called it "unfortunate" that ChemoCentryx did not disclose its actions to the FDA, noting that Amgen itself had been in the dark. Tavneos was intended to replace or reduce the use of steroids, which AAV patients may need for months to years. Since the drug reached the market, it has been linked to eight deaths and dozens of hospitalizations, according to Ars Technica. The United Kingdom has announced it will also remove the product from the market. The case also highlights how incentives differ between small biotechs and large pharmaceutical companies. Sean Nicholson, an economist at Cornell University, told Undark that a significant number of FDA-approved drugs start at small companies with few or no marketed products, and that large firms increasingly buy or partner with nimble startups rather than develop breakthrough science themselves. David Ridley, a health economist at Duke University's Fuqua School of Business, said small companies face a different set of incentives: a large company with many pipeline products may more readily abandon an experimental drug than fund costly late-stage testing. One advisory committee participant told Undark the 2021 vote was "based upon an assumption that the sponsor was following the rules of the road." The FDA's proposal to withdraw approval is not the final step. Amgen's response is now before the agency, and the outcome will determine whether Tavneos remains available in the US. The case tests whether the FDA can unwind an approval years after the fact when the underlying trial data are disputed. For Amgen, Tavneos is a product with nearly half a billion dollars in annual sales and a multibillion-dollar acquisition behind it. For AAV patients, withdrawal would remove a steroid-sparing option, though the drug has also been linked to eight deaths and dozens of hospitalizations. For smaller biotechs, the episode sharpens scrutiny of how trial data are handled before a large company acquires the asset. The FDA will weigh Amgen's 104-page response before deciding whether to finalize withdrawal. Amgen has distanced itself from ChemoCentryx's conduct, which could shape whether the agency treats the issue as a company-specific violation or a broader data-integrity problem. The proposed $69 million investor-lawsuit settlement, subject to the October 29 hearing, may also produce further disclosures. The UK's removal decision adds pressure but does not bind the FDA. title: Justice Department Moves to Set Aside Alaska Ballots in Criminal Probe of Senate Candidate
description: Federal prosecutors want certain ballots isolated while they investigate whether voters were confused by a Senate candidate who shares the Republican incumbent's name.
body: The U.S. Department of Justice asked a court Friday to set aside certain Alaska ballots as part of an investigation into potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed a criminal probe involving a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, NPR reported. Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been running for several months. He pointed to recent reporting by The New York Times indicating that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run. That candidate shares a name with incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. Heyman declined to say what crimes authorities are examining or who the targets are. He asked the public to come forward with tips. It is highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm one exists. The department also filed a list of proposed questions it wants to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer. Those questions belong to a civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he directed the department to file that case. Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot. "I am not interested in tricking voters," she said. At a campaign rally in Anchorage late Friday, she said she is "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy," adding that she does not need help winning beyond the support of voters. Asked before the rally whether someone on her campaign could have been involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, she told KTUU: "I have no idea." An FBI agent visited a boat dealership in the candidate's hometown of Petersburg, according to its owner, who had donated to Dan J. Sullivan's campaign. The owner told The Associated Press the agent asked whether he had been misled by the candidacy; he said he had not, adding that people know who the incumbent is. Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a "substantial risk" that Dan J. Sullivan could be confused with the incumbent. Attorneys for the candidate, according to the reporting, have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The request to segregate ballots in Alaska follows a decision by the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejecting the Justice Department's request that California set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election and sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. The timing of Friday's press conference is notable. The Justice Department has a longstanding practice of avoiding public steps in the weeks before an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome. The Alaska race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate. Trump, speaking at a rally in Florida late Friday, referenced Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan. According to the reporting, he said: "OK, he said 'yes.'" The context of that remark was not fully described in the account. The state Division of Elections, in a letter dated Monday, said it signs agreements with local or tribal offices to run voting sites and that most of the 18 sites flagged in the reporting had opened. The account did not elaborate on which sites were at issue. The sequence leaves several open questions. The department has confirmed a criminal investigation but not its scope, potential charges or targets. The civil case and the criminal probe are proceeding on separate tracks, and it is not clear how a court will rule on the request to isolate ballots or on the candidate's motion to dismiss. Peltola has denied knowledge of any recruitment effort, while the Times reporting described campaign involvement that she has not confirmed. A public criminal probe and a ballot-segregation request in a Senate race that could decide chamber control put prosecutors' actions directly into an election's final days. That affects Alaska voters, both campaigns and the Justice Department's own norm of avoiding pre-election public steps. If a court grants the segregation request, it creates a mechanism for disputing results after the vote; if it refuses, the department's leverage narrows. title: UK Budget: Energy Bill Help, Pension Rise and the ISA U-Turn Explained
description: A £300-plus January energy bill increase looms, VAT on electricity is extended to July, gas standing charges are set to go, and the cash ISA cut is scrapped.
body: Households are being offered help with rising prices at the same time as annual energy bills are forecast to climb by around £300 or more in January, according to BBC Business. The Budget measures described by the BBC cover pay, energy, savings, motoring costs, pensions and student loans, and several of them arrive after the point when bills are expected to rise. On energy, tariffs linked to regulator Ofgem's price cap are forecast to rise by hundreds of pounds a year, reaching an annual bill of £2,000 or more in January. The VAT cut on electricity bills, introduced in October, will be extended to July; it had been due to end in April. Fixed daily gas fees will be abolished in England, Scotland and Wales during 2027, or as soon as practicable after that date according to the chancellor, and replaced by higher charges per unit of energy consumed. The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will gain an average of £45 a year from that shift, with lower users gaining the most. The BBC reports that the gain will not arrive until after the projected big rise in bills in January. Higher users, including people in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families, will pay more than they do currently. Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive equivalent funding and will decide whether to introduce the same payment, the BBC reports. The BBC describes the support as designed to help with soaring energy bills. On pay, the BBC reports that any kind of pay rise could drag a worker into a higher tax bracket, or mean a greater proportion of income is taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands. The BBC does not, in the supplied material, set out the specific thresholds or rates behind that warning, so the precise scale of the effect for any given worker is not established here. On savings, the chancellor has abandoned a plan drawn up by his predecessor to lower the ceiling on tax-free cash holdings in Individual Savings Accounts. Rachel Reeves had argued the restriction would nudge savers toward stocks and shares. Under the original design, from April 2027 savers under 65 would have faced a £12,000 annual cash limit instead of the existing £20,000. That proposal is now off the table, so the larger cash allowance survives. On motoring, the BBC reports that a planned change to a fuel levy was scheduled to be phased out from January, but drivers will still pay the levy at 52p per litre. The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February, according to the report. On pensions, the triple lock will lift the state pension by 3.9%, tracking average wage growth. The chancellor said the arrangement would hold until at least 2030, and that a new Pension Tax Allowance would exempt pensioners whose income does not exceed the full new state pension from income tax. On housing, the chancellor confirmed the Your First Home equity scheme, which will allow first-time buyers in England to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. Under the scheme, buyers would receive a loan covering a fifth of the property's value to put toward the purchase. On student loans, the BBC reports criticism of a decision by the previous chancellor to hold down the Plan 2 repayment threshold. Plan 2 loans were issued in England over a little more than a decade from 2012. The salary at which borrowers begin repaying, £29,385, is due to stay at that level in April and to remain there for three years. The practical effect is that graduates cross into repayment sooner and see larger monthly deductions than they would under a threshold that moved with earnings. The BBC notes that some announcements affecting personal finances had previously been made by the government. It also points readers to their annual bill or the government's website to find their council tax band, adding that the website was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement. The package mixes immediate relief with delayed effects. The VAT extension on electricity runs to July, while the gas standing charge change is not expected until 2027. The £45 average gain for 60% of households is a Treasury calculation and lands after the January bill increase the BBC describes. For lower energy users the shift in how gas is charged may help; for higher users, including large low-income families, the same change works the other way. The cash ISA decision removes a planned restriction rather than adding a new benefit, and the pension and first-home measures set out longer-run changes to tax and deposit requirements. What the BBC's account does not provide is the full fiscal cost of these measures, the detailed distributional analysis beyond the Treasury's £45 figure, or confirmation of how the devolved administrations will use equivalent funding. The measures change what households pay and keep at the margins: energy standing charges move from fixed daily fees to unit prices, the electricity VAT cut lasts longer, the cash ISA limit stays at £20,000, and the state pension rises 3.9%. The timing matters most. The Treasury's £45 average gain for 60% of households arrives after a January bill increase the BBC puts at around £300 or more, so many households may see costs rise before they see the offset. Higher gas users, including large low-income families, face higher bills under the standing-charge shift. The January energy price cap change is the next hard data point, followed by the April student loan threshold and the July end of the extended electricity VAT cut. The gas standing charge change is expected in 2027 or as soon as possible after. Devolved administrations must decide whether to mirror the support payment. title: Obsidian Canvas and Heptabase: How File-First and Card-First Design Shape Spatial Notes
description: A comparison of the two tools' data models finds that Obsidian stores visual arrangements in standalone .canvas files, while Heptabase treats whiteboards as views over a central card library.
body: Obsidian Canvas and Heptabase both let users arrange notes on a two-dimensional whiteboard, but the two tools store those arrangements in opposite ways, according to a comparison published by fluxlinks.com on October 28, 2026. The article argues that the difference matters more than any feature checklist: Obsidian Canvas keeps visual layouts inside individual .canvas files written in the open JSON Canvas format, while Heptabase treats whiteboards as non-owning visual views over a central card library. The distinction begins with what each tool treats as its basic unit. Obsidian is built on a local-first philosophy in which a knowledge base is a folder of plain-text Markdown files, the article states. Obsidian chose the file as its atomic unit, a decision the article credits for making a vault portable and durable. It is also why, in the article's account, a canvas can only be another file, with nowhere to store a connection except inside itself. When a user creates an Obsidian Canvas, the result is a standalone .canvas file stored on disk as JSON. That storage model has visible consequences for notes created directly on a canvas. If a user types ten quick thought cards directly onto an Obsidian Canvas, those cards exist only inside that .canvas file, according to the article. They do not appear as independent notes in the vault unless the user manually converts them into separate Markdown files one at a time. External notes placed on a canvas are embedded views: the canvas references the file's path from the outside. When the same note is opened in Obsidian's regular editor, it does not display which canvases currently contain it, and it does not know which neighboring cards sit next to it on any canvas. Heptabase separates what a note is from where a note is viewed, the article states. Its atomic unit is the card rather than the file. Whiteboard lines provide what the article calls a dedicated spatial linking layer that cards track wherever they are opened, while inline @mentions in card text handle linear cross-references. The practical difference the article highlights is that a line drawn on an Obsidian Canvas creates no link between notes in the vault, whereas a line drawn on a Heptabase whiteboard creates a connection both cards remember. The article also says a card in Heptabase can show every whiteboard that currently contains it. The comparison extends to portability. Obsidian's connections are described as portable across external tools but unindexed in the vault's graph; Heptabase's connections are described as indexed across cards but locked into its proprietary ecosystem. The article says the same .md note file can be embedded across multiple .canvas files, and any text edits made to that note stay in sync. Adopting Heptabase, by contrast, requires committing to a specialized, proprietary ecosystem rather than relying on standard plain-text files, according to the article. The article also raises limits that apply to spatial tools generally, not only to one product. It says 2D arrows lack explicit logical semantics: an arrow between Card A and Card B indicates a connection but not logic, and does not formally specify whether an idea supports a claim, refutes an assumption, or serves as a prerequisite condition. It also points to translation friction from 2D space to linear prose, noting that whiteboards arrange thoughts across spatial coordinates while essays, reports and memos are read sequentially. Bridging messy exploration and rigorous writing, in the article's view, requires modeling the logical dependencies of ideas—claims, evidence and counterarguments—rather than 2D coordinates. The article's central recommendation is that users deciding where to build a long-term knowledge workflow should look at how each tool models files, cards and context rather than at interface features. It frames the choice as one between a file-centric architecture that keeps data in open, portable files and a card-centric architecture that indexes connections across a proprietary system. The piece also poses, as a question, whether Obsidian Canvas is fully offline and local-first compared with Heptabase, without the supplied excerpt resolving that point. The comparison does not include pricing, performance benchmarks, user counts or independent testing of either product. Its claims rest on how the two systems are described to store and link data. For readers weighing the tools, the reported trade-off is concrete: Obsidian's approach keeps canvases as files that other tools can read, at the cost of connections that the vault's graph does not index and notes that live only inside a canvas unless converted. Heptabase's approach keeps connections visible from the cards themselves, at the cost of depending on a proprietary ecosystem rather than plain-text files. The choice affects anyone building a long-term notes or research system. A file-centric design keeps data readable by other tools and durable if a product changes, but connections drawn on a canvas stay inside that canvas file and are not indexed in the vault's graph. A card-centric design makes those connections visible from every card, which helps retrieval, but ties the workflow to a proprietary system. The trade-off shapes switching costs, how easily notes can be reused, and how much of a user's thinking remains legible outside the app. Expect continued debate over open formats versus integrated linking as note tools compete on how they model connections. Obsidian's JSON Canvas format gives other tools a path to read canvas files, while Heptabase's card model may appeal to users who prioritize cross-whiteboard links. Neither approach resolves the article's broader point that 2D arrows do not encode logical relationships, so users may still need separate methods to move from exploration to structured writing. title: Lula Wins Historic Fourth Term as Brazil's President, Defeating Flávio Bolsonaro
description: With 100% of votes counted, Lula took 51.79% to Flávio Bolsonaro's 48.21%, a margin of 4.4 million votes. Bolsonaro refused to concede and said his legal team would seek to annul the result.
body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a historic fourth term as Brazil's president, defeating the far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, according to The Guardian. With 100% of votes counted, the 80-year-old leftist took 51.79% of the vote to his 45-year-old rival's 48.21%, a margin of 4.4 million votes. The Guardian reports that Brazil's electoral authority confirmed the result, completing a turnaround from the first round earlier in October. The campaign's first round, in early October, went against Lula: he narrowly lost to Flávio Bolsonaro, plunging progressive Brazilians into what The Guardian described as three weeks of despair. The second-round reversal is, by the outlet's account, without precedent since democracy returned to Brazil in the 1980s — never before had a first-round runner-up gone on to win the second vote. Lula's victory speech, delivered to a packed crowd of supporters in a São Paulo conference hall, framed the outcome in broad terms. He said his government would change the way the country is governed, called the election a defeat for denialism, thanked God and the Brazilian people, and said it was democracy that made the result happen. Flávio Bolsonaro said during Lula’s victory speech that he could not concede and that his legal team would seek annulment. He objected to Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting by two hours, to 7pm, describing it as a change in the rules during the contest. The Guardian notes that Bolsonaro’s own campaign had also requested an extension. His announced intention to challenge the outcome is separate from any decision by a court to alter the reported result. Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. The Guardian reports that Jair lost the 2022 election to Lula and was subsequently jailed for plotting a coup. The younger Bolsonaro’s challenge concerns the new election, rather than that earlier contest. BBC News traces Lula’s rise from a childhood of poverty to metalworking and trade-union leadership. Before becoming a politician, he sold peanuts and shined shoes, learned to read at 10 and later trained for industrial work near São Paulo. A workplace accident in the 1960s cost him the little finger of his left hand. In 1975 he was elected to lead the Metalworkers’ Union, with roughly 100,000 members. The BBC describes his role in making it a more independent force. He helped found the Workers’ Party in 1980 with unionists, intellectuals and Church activists. The party later moved toward a more pragmatic social-democratic programme, according to the profile. After losing presidential bids in 1989, 1994 and 1998, Lula won in 2002. His first two terms ran from 2003 to 2010. The BBC associates that period with expanded social programmes, minimum-wage increases above inflation and the Bolsa Família family grant. It reports that the assistance reached about 44 million people and helped underpin his support among poorer Brazilians. The profile also records criticism that those programmes did not resolve deeper causes of poverty, including inadequate education. At the end of the two terms, the BBC puts his popularity at 83% and describes a sustained period of economic growth and greater international prominence for Brazil. Lula’s political return also followed imprisonment and overturned convictions. According to the BBC, he maintained his innocence and called the accusations politically motivated. He was released in 2019 after just over 18 months, following a Supreme Court ruling concerning imprisonment before appeals were exhausted. His convictions were annulled in 2021, allowing him to contest the 2022 election against Jair Bolsonaro. When he returned to office in 2023, he said it would be his last term. The Workers’ Party nevertheless endorsed him again in 2026. He turns 81 on Tuesday, the BBC reports. Policy questions accompany the win. The BBC reports that Lula's support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon has drawn criticism. Lula insists he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy. His government has pointed to reduced deforestation in the Amazon, with satellite data suggesting the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was the lowest in the past decade, as proof its policies were working. The BBC also describes Brazil’s participation in Brics and Lula’s defence of continued ties with Russia and China. He regards that grouping as a potential counterweight to Western influence, according to the profile. International reaction was quick. Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum said democracy had won and congratulated Lula, while Paraguayan president Santiago Peña saluted the Brazilian people for what he called a great democratic journey, according to The Guardian. The Guardian describes a first-round runner-up overturning the earlier order in a presidential runoff for the first time in Brazil’s modern democratic era. The reported complete count gives Lula another mandate, while Flávio Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede raises the prospect of further political or legal dispute. The next term also brings questions over Amazon policy, oil exploration and international alignment. Lula’s preparations for a new term and the response of political and international partners may show how the contest moves from election night into governing. title: Paulina Borsook's 'Cyberselfish' Returns in New Tin House Edition
description: TechCrunch reports that the 2000 book on techno-libertarian culture is coming back into print, with the author reflecting on Silicon Valley's leadership class and AI in a new interview.
body: Paulina Borsook's "Cyberselfish," a book first published in 2000 that went out of print, is returning in a new edition from Tin House, TechCrunch reported on October 25, 2026, in an article by Anthony Ha. The announcement arrives after a period in which the book drew renewed attention from readers and commentators seeking to understand how the technology industry "lost its way," according to the TechCrunch account. TechCrunch interviewed Borsook over Zoom about the book’s revival and her interpretation of technology-industry culture. The interview provides her account of the ideas and workplace attitudes she set out to examine. Borsook described the book's purpose in the interview as being "almost a travelogue" of her efforts to understand what she calls the techno-libertarian influence on Silicon Valley culture. She said she began moving through tech circles in the Bay Area in the early-to-middle 1980s, and that starting around the early 1990s she began hearing offhand remarks from some people that struck her as strange and that she could not make sense of. Those remarks, as she frames it, became the raw material for an attempt to map a set of beliefs rather than to write a conventional corporate history. A central distinction in the book, as Borsook described it to TechCrunch, is between what she calls "Ravers" and "Gilders." The Gilders, in her account, are social conservatives, named after George Gilder, whom she described in sharply critical terms as a conservative and reactionary thought leader of the early 1990s. The Ravers, named in homage to John Perry Barlow, she associated with drugs, sex and rock and roll, a Burning Man sensibility and a more culturally liberal outlook. The point of the pairing, as she presents it, is that both currents coexisted inside the same industry culture, and that the libertarian strain she was trying to describe was not simply a matter of electoral affiliation. On that question, Borsook was careful to separate culture from party politics. She noted that the San Francisco Peninsula still votes Democratic and that Ro Khanna is the area's congressman, and said she was really talking about culture rather than electoral politics. Her focus, she said, was the leadership class in tech, the people she calls the tech overlords, and she added that it is not so clear to her how much the rank and file share those attitudes, though she suspects probably more than when she was more familiar with the region. Borsook also described employment insecurity as a reason some workers accommodate views they do not share. In her account, employees may decide to keep a job or a project while distancing themselves privately from the beliefs of their employers. She treated that compromise as a continuing workplace pattern, rather than a wholly new development. Borsook criticizes a philosophy she considers strongly opposed to regulation. She told TechCrunch that the industry’s reliance on public research and development is missing from that account of its success. These are central arguments in her interpretation of the sector, rather than claims established by new research presented with the reissue. Looking back, Borsook told TechCrunch that she sees more continuity than change. She pointed to the Netscape initial public offering as the moment things really began to change, describing Silicon Valley as having been invaded by finance professionals and a culture of flipping and fleeing. Even after the dot-com crash, she said, that attitude remained, percolating and spreading. She acknowledged, with what she called good reason, that a great deal of wonderful technology came out of the era and its successors, and said she would never deny that. Her criticism, she emphasized, concerns business culture and how industry leaders see themselves, rather than a denial that useful technologies emerged. Borsook also applied her criticism to AI. In the TechCrunch interview, she compared the present AI moment to a Ponzi scheme. That was the author’s polemical characterization, not a legal or regulatory finding. Her remarks place current arguments over AI inside the longer critique of industry values she developed for the original book. TechCrunch traces the revival to a sequence of events. Last year, Gil Durán, author of "Nerd Reich," publicly argued that it was time to revive Borsook's career, saying she "saw it all very clearly and tried to warn us 25 years ago." Later that fall, The New York Times reported that "Cyberselfish" was finding new fans interested in why the tech industry had drifted from its earlier promise. Borsook told TechCrunch that she began noticing used copies of the book commanding rising prices, along with unexpected social media posts from people she did not know describing the book as important, and inquiries from European academics. That attention, she said, eventually led to more press coverage and to the new Tin House edition, which includes a new introduction by Durán. The returning edition gives a 2000 critique of Silicon Valley’s libertarian strain a new readership amid debate over AI, regulation and industry power. Borsook’s account also describes interest spreading through readers, academics and press coverage. Attention may turn to Durán’s introduction and to how Borsook’s older critique is received in current debates over AI and regulation. Future reviews and interviews could show whether interest extends beyond the initial wave of readers and academics described in the TechCrunch report. title: Data centre backlash grows as AI demand reshapes towns and grids
description: BBC reporting describes concern over power, water and noise alongside claims of jobs and tax revenue. A separate Apollo economist's assessment adds context on corporate AI returns.
body: Data centres have become the quiet infrastructure behind nearly every routine online activity, from search queries and email to streaming video and banking. According to BBC News, these warehouse-like buildings are also central to the artificial intelligence boom, housing the advanced chips and servers that run services such as ChatGPT and Claude. As the facilities grow larger and more numerous, the BBC reports that a backlash is building in communities that host them or are being asked to. The BBC cites Data Center Map, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites, in putting the global count at about 12,250 data centres. The geography is uneven. The United States has the densest concentration, with 4,767 sites, followed by Europe, where the United Kingdom and Germany lead. Historically, the BBC notes, data centres have tended to sit near cities, where access to high-voltage power lines or water for cooling is easier. As the buildings get bigger, more are being sited in rural areas, shifting the debate from urban industrial zones to smaller communities. The BBC's example of scale is Colossus 2, part of the wider Colossus campus, which is expected to house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and to be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company plans to use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site. Activists quoted by the BBC say the turbines could "significantly increase" local air pollution, while local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards. The BBC juxtaposes the activists’ pollution concerns with regulators’ statements about air-quality standards. The BBC identifies resource pressure as a central driver of concern. Data centres can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which some experts say could lead to shortages. Their electricity demand is also growing, which the BBC says is driving up carbon emissions according to analysis, and putting pressure on local grids. Some fear that strain could push up energy prices. Political pressure is following. The BBC reports that 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and that the issue could be a key one in November's midterm elections. Outside the United States, the BBC says opposition has emerged in countries including Mexico, France, Indonesia and the UK. The US measures are reported as proposals, rather than bans already in force. Industry advocates push back. The BBC notes that supporters say data centres are good for the economy, attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas such as construction. The BBC also cites a recent report by the Brookings Center suggesting that data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim. The type of facility matters, according to that research: so-called hyperscale sites, massive facilities owned and run by tech giants such as Amazon and Microsoft, were found to have a bigger positive effect on jobs, while "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits. In separate reporting on corporate AI adoption, TechCrunch described a note by Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, arguing that promised financial benefits have not appeared in the operating measures he examined. Slok focused on what he calls the S&P 493, the S&P 500 minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla, and found that profit margins and revenue per worker appeared flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity. TechCrunch reports that Slok sounded skeptical about whether corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins. His assessment concerns the operating measures of that company grouping, rather than a calculation of returns for individual data-centre projects. Taken together, the BBC reporting describes a planning and consent problem as much as a technology story. Facilities that power everyday internet use and AI services need land, power and water, and those needs are increasingly visible to neighbours. The BBC's account sets local environmental and cost concerns against industry arguments about investment, tax revenue and jobs, with regulators defending air-quality compliance at the Colossus site. The Brookings findings add nuance by suggesting that the local economic benefit depends on the kind of facility and its ties to the community, rather than being uniform across the sector. Data centres are the physical layer beneath AI and everyday internet services, so disputes over power, water, noise and local costs now shape whether and where digital infrastructure gets built. The BBC report shows the argument moving from technical planning to state legislatures and elections, while industry and regulators defend economic and air-quality claims. Watch whether the 16 state proposals advance into law or stall, how the issue surfaces in November's midterms, and whether operators adjust siting, cooling or power arrangements in response to local objections.
